Q: How to convert a dict into a pandas multiindex dataframe A:

I think the format of the data is fine. You just need to unpack it correctly to get a useable dataframe.

  • Construct a dataframe from the dict values and dict keys.
  • Unpack the level of the index with the element names to two columns.
  • Apply crosstab with the appropriate index and columns (apply .fillna(0) to the result to get the exact same structure as in your question).
df = pd.DataFrame(my_dict.values(), pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(my_dict.keys()))
df[['first_element', 'second_element']] = df.index.get_level_values(1).to_list()
pd.crosstab(
    [df.index.get_level_values(0), df.first_element],
    df.second_element,
    values=df[0],
    aggfunc='sum')

Q: How StateFlow.collectAsState() works A:

A Flow in general is an observable stream of values. That is compatible to the concept of Compose State, which represents a value that can be observed for changes. collectAsState1 simply converts a Flow into a Compose State.

That means that whenever the Flow emits2 a new value, the corresponding State object changes its value and triggers a recomposition. That works because internally, collectAsState launches a coroutine to wait for new values. That coroutine is usually suspended most of the time and only wakes up when a new value was emitted into the Flow. It receives the new value in a callback and updates the Compose State object, which in turn triggers a recomposition, keeping the UI up-to-date.

Your assumption is basically correct, except that collectAsState doesn't actively access the value property, it receives the new value in a callback. But that are details that doesn't matter when you just use the function.

1 As a reminder, when you use any other Flow implementation than a MutableStateFlow you should use collectAsStateWithLifecycle instead of collectAsState, that saves resources by stopping the Flow when it isn't needed. You don't need that for a MutableStateFlow because that is special in that it isn't running its own coroutine to produce values, so there is nothing that needs be stopped. Its probably easier to always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle though, the overhead is minimal and you decouple your Compose code from the view model implementation.

2 The MutableStateFlow you use emits a new value whenever you write to the value property or use the update method. StateFlows have the additional semantic that they drop redundant values. So if you write the same value again, nothing happens.

Q: Nested dictionary to multiindex dataframe where dictionary keys are column labels A:

Pandas wants the MultiIndex values as tuples, not nested dicts. The simplest thing is to convert your dictionary to the right format before trying to pass it to DataFrame:

>>> reform = {
...     (outerKey, innerKey): values
...     for outerKey, innerDict in dictionary.items()
...     for innerKey, values in innerDict.items()}
>>> reform
{('A', 'a'): [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
 ('A', 'b'): [6, 7, 8, 9, 1],
 ('B', 'a'): [2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
 ('B', 'b'): [7, 8, 9, 1, 2]}
>>> pandas.DataFrame(reform)
   A     B   
   a  b  a  b
0  1  6  2  7
1  2  7  3  8
2  3  8  4  9
3  4  9  5  1
4  5  1  6  2

[5 rows x 4 columns]

Q: How to intercept PreparedStatement and reconstruct SQL with parameters using Byte Buddy for GBase 8c JDBC driver? A:

To debug such a scenario, simply add a breakpoint within the implementation you are instrumenting. Use your debugger to poke at the reachable objects, fields and parameters. Byte Buddy can not give you access to anything more. Possibly, you have to instrument more methods and save it in a context object, if you cannot otherwise reach it.

Q: Multiple apk support for Android TV and Phone A:

You can publish separate APKs for Android TV and phones by using different device configurations and version codes while keeping the same package name. For TV-focused apps, you can also check Tuper TV for an example of an Android TV app experience.

Q: How can I rename all files in a directory to have an equal number of digits? A:

There's a tool named rename that comes with File::Rename, and there are other versions of rename too. Since you requirements are simple,

$ ls 
image1.jpg  image2.jpg  image920.jpg

The -n switch does a dry run. In this example, I match the run of digits in each name and in the replacement side of the substitution I format that however I need. In this case, I format it to have three digits and pad with 0s. Since I want to run Perl code in the replacement side, I use the /e flag (for eval):

$ rename -n 's/(\d+)(?=\.jpg\z)/sprintf q(%03d), $1/e' *.jpg
rename image1.jpg image001.jpg
rename image2.jpg image002.jpg

Notice there's not output for image920.jpg because its name would not change.

When I'm satisfied I like the transformations, I leave off the -n:

$ rename 's/(\d+)(?=\.jpg\z)/sprintf q(%03d), $1/e' *.jpg
$ ls
image001.jpg    image002.jpg    image920.jpg

You have to choose the width, but you probably don't really care what the length actually is as long as the next tool understands the sequence.

Q: Writing just one line to fifo A:

This is a race condition, not a Rust issue.

fh is closed at the end of each loop iteration, but the next open() can happen before cat gets scheduled and notices that there are no writers. In that case, cat keeps reading more Hello lines instead of seeing EOF.

That also explains why strace or a short sleep changes the behavior: they slow the writer down enough for cat to observe EOF.

The occasional BrokenPipe happens when cat closes the FIFO after open() succeeds but before write_all() runs.

A FIFO does not provide one independent connection per reader. If you need exactly one response per client invocation without sleeps, a Unix-domain socket is a better fit.
